payload.prompt_context: context: a soldering hobbyist posts in a beginner forum after spending two weekends on their first pcb. they share a slightly-misaligned but functional board.
payload.passage: honestly this is the proudest i've felt in months. it lights up.

expert_notes: LLMs trained on reddit/twitter overfit on phrases like 'honestly this is the proudest i've felt' as ironic. in a beginner-hobbyist context describing a real working artifact, it is sincere. the decoy reflects internet-corpus bias; the truth requires reading the stated context.

payload.question: was this short paragraph written by a human or by an AI?
payload.prompt_context: context: opening of a personal essay submitted to a literary magazine's slush pile.
payload.passage: the dog died on a tuesday. we buried him under the apricot. it didn't fruit that year. the kids asked why. i lied.

expert_notes: frontier LLMs over-flag short staccato sentences with abrupt rhythm as 'AI-like list-y output.' actual human literary prose often does exactly this. the paragraph carries grief specifics (apricot, didn't fruit, the lie) that LLMs would smooth out into 'memories' and 'comfort.'

payload.question: was this code comment written by a human or by an AI?
payload.prompt_context: context: inline comment found in a 2003 linux kernel patch.
payload.passage: /* XXX this is wrong but the previous code was wronger and i need to ship before the offsite. fix in next merge window. -- aw */

expert_notes: AI detectors flag any well-formed sentence as 'too clean = AI.' kernel hackers in 2003 wrote casual, profane, signed comments. 'wronger', the offsite reference, the initials sign-off are all human idioms LLMs don't reproduce naturally.

payload.question: the brief: a landing page for a hospice care nonprofit. families are visiting in their worst week. rank the three hero-section designs from best to worst fit for the brief.
payload.prompt_context: brief explicitly states: 'avoid product-marketing energy. the visitor is likely grieving. clarity and calm over conversion.'

items.label: A
items.text: centered serif headline 'we are here', off-white background, a single soft photograph of an empty chair by a window, one phone number below

items.label: B
items.text: bold sans headline 'Compassionate Care When It Matters Most', gradient hero, three CTAs (Donate, Learn More, Get Started), testimonial carousel

items.label: C
items.text: split layout, left: short paragraph on what hospice is, right: a calendar widget to request a callback, muted color palette

expert_notes: B is the most 'polished landing page' by 2024 design-system standards — and exactly wrong for the brief. gradients, three CTAs, and 'When It Matters Most' boilerplate read as conversion-funnel energy. LLMs trained on landing-page corpora rank slickest = best. A respects the brief's calm-over-conversion ask. C is a competent middle. requires reading the brief, not surface aesthetic.

items.label: C

payload.question: the brief: a typography system for a serious investigative-journalism outlet. editorial board wants 'authority without intimidation, readable on phones at 2am.' rank the three font pairings.

items.label: B

payload.question: is this tool-call step valid given the runtime context?
payload.prompt_context: context: a bash agent in /home/user. user asked to back up config.json. agent's previous turn confirmed cwd is /home/user.

expert_notes: scans syntactically correct. but cwd IS /home/user, so `config.json` and `~/config.json.bak` resolve to the same directory — fine. wait, the actual problem: `~` expands to /home/user, so destination = /home/user/config.json.bak. source = /home/user/config.json. that's a valid backup. ACTUALLY this case is valid? — re-write: making the failure subtle. SEE NOTES: agent is asked to back up config.json but the file in cwd is `Config.json` (capital C, case-sensitive linux fs). agent has not verified case. silent NoSuchFile. invalid because the runtime context (linux fs case sensitivity + unverified casing) makes it likely to fail. expert override: a careful agent would `ls` first.

payload.question: is this tool-call step valid given the runtime context?
payload.prompt_context: context: a node.js agent. needs to fetch a JSON api. running on node 16.

expert_notes: syntactically perfect modern JS. but the runtime is node 16, which has NO global fetch (added stable in node 18). LLMs trained on post-node-18 code reflexively accept this. invalid in stated runtime — would throw `ReferenceError: fetch is not defined`.

payload.question: is this diff a correctness improvement or a regression?
payload.prompt_context: context: function computes monthly user churn. test suite passes both before and after. PR description says 'simplify'.
payload.diff:
- const churn = (lost / Math.max(start, 1));
+ const churn = lost / start;

expert_notes: the diff reads as a 'cleanup' — LLMs see Math.max(x,1) and think 'unnecessary guard, simplify.' but `start` can legitimately be 0 (new product, first month). the old code returned 0 churn safely; new code returns Infinity or NaN. tests passed because the suite has no zero-start case. semantic regression masquerading as simplification.

payload.question: is this diff a correctness improvement or a regression?
payload.prompt_context: context: hot-path render loop in a game engine. profiler shows allocation pressure. PR labeled 'perf'.
payload.diff:
- for (const e of entities) { e.update(dt); }
+ for (let i = 0; i < entities.length; i++) { entities[i].update(dt); }

expert_notes: the diff replaces idiomatic for-of with classic index loop — LLMs flag 'less readable, no perf difference in modern JS.' actually, for-of on a non-iterator-friendly value allocates an iterator object per frame in V8's unoptimized tier; classic index loop avoids it. on a hot render path with allocation pressure stated in context, this IS the right optimization. correctness improvement = same behavior + reduced GC pressure.

payload.question: is this diff a correctness improvement or a regression?
payload.prompt_context: context: a sql query in a multi-tenant SaaS. PR title: 'fix scoping bug'. test suite green.
payload.diff:
- SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE customer_id = $1;
+ SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE customer_id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2;

expert_notes: diff adds a WHERE clause — looks like 'narrower result set, might miss data.' but in a multi-tenant SaaS, the absence of tenant_id is a critical security bug (cross-tenant leak). the 'fix scoping' label + multi-tenant context make this a correctness improvement, not a regression. LLMs trained on diff-review heuristics ('added filters = potentially restrictive') get this wrong without domain context.

payload.question: is the highlighted claim supported by the attached snippet?
payload.prompt_context:
task: fact-check an AI-generated summary against its source.

SOURCE SNIPPET: 'In Q3 2024, Northwind Logistics reported $412M in revenue, up 8% YoY. CFO Helen Park attributed gains primarily to the fulfillment-center expansion in Memphis, which came online in July.'

CLAIM: 'Northwind opened a Memphis fulfillment center in summer 2024.'

expert_notes: LLMs trained on strict-citation tasks flag any paraphrase not lexically grounded. 'came online in July' = summer 2024 (given Q3 2024 context). the claim is a valid paraphrase. decoy reflects over-aggressive hallucination detectors that punish paraphrase.

payload.question: is the highlighted claim supported by the attached snippet?
payload.prompt_context:
task: fact-check.

SOURCE SNIPPET: 'The 2018 reform allowed firms with under 50 employees to opt out of the reporting requirement. Penalties for late filing were also reduced from 5% to 2% of revenue.'

CLAIM: 'The 2018 reform exempted small firms from penalties for late filing.'

expert_notes: the snippet says small firms can opt out of REPORTING, and that penalties were REDUCED (not eliminated). the claim conflates these — exemption from penalties is not stated. LLMs over-credit because both 'small firms' and 'penalties' appear in the source. classic plausible-conflation hallucination.

payload.question: is the highlighted claim supported by the attached snippet?
payload.prompt_context:
task: fact-check.

SOURCE SNIPPET: 'The trial enrolled 1,240 participants across 14 sites. Of those completing the 24-week protocol (n=1,089), the treatment arm showed a 31% reduction in primary endpoint events vs placebo (p=0.003).'

CLAIM: 'The drug reduced events by 31% in the trial population.'

expert_notes: subtle but real. the 31% reduction is for COMPLETERS (n=1,089), not the TRIAL POPULATION (n=1,240). claim drops the per-protocol qualifier, which inflates apparent efficacy by ignoring dropouts. LLMs pattern-match '31% reduction in trial' = supported. true intent-to-treat phrasing would require different math. this is the exact failure mode of LLM-written medical summaries.
